The Vessantara Jātaka 1:
The Story of the Ten Boons “Phussatī,
of excellent complexion and radiance...”
Choose ten boons,
O lady of lovely limbs, whatever is dear to your heart from this earth.”
“O King of Devas, let there be homage to you!
What evil have I committed that you have driven me away from this delightful place?”
“Like the wind [shaking] a tree.
“You have committed no evil,
nor am you unloved by me;”
Your merit has been completely exhausted,
which is why I speak to you thus:
death is near for you.
There will be separation;
please accept these from me as I grant you ten boons.”
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka,
Lord of all beings, then, O Blessed One,
[grant it] to King Sivi.”
There, in my dwelling,
was a woman with blue eyes, blue eyebrows,
and blue lashes, like a doe.
There, O Purindada, you shall see her named Phussatī;
she will obtain a son who is a giver of boons.
He was devoted to giving, free from stinginess,
honored by rival kings,
renowned, and illustrious.
As I bear a child in my womb,
my waist is not prominent;
may my belly likewise remain unprotruded.
Like a well-drawn bow, it is perfectly straight.
O Vāsava, may my limbs not fall away, nor may my hair turn grey.
Dust shall not cling to his body,
and he may even release one condemned to death,
amidst the cries of peacocks and cranes.
It was filled with throngs of excellent women, crowded with hunchbacks, female slaves, and porters,
and resounded with the songs of bards and panegyrists.
O venerable one, you who were smeared with red lead and vermilion, and who were awakened by wine and meat—
[this was] for the sake of King Śibi.
“Then she shall be my beloved queen.
“Those ten boons which were granted by me,
O you who are beautiful in every limb,”
"In the realm of King Sivi,
you shall receive all those boons.
Having said this, Maghavā—
Sujampati, the king of the gods,
having granted a boon to Phussatī,
Vāsava expressed his appreciation.
The Discourse on the Ten Qualities, titled "The Ten":
"With hair growing long in the armpits and on the body,
with teeth stained by grime and veins showing;"
“Having raised his right arm,
what do the brahmins ask of me?
“We ask for a jewel, O King.”
The increaser of the Sivi kingdom’s realm;
give me that excellent elephant,
with tusks like chariot-poles and a broad back.”
“I give and do not waver when brahmins ask me for [my son],
who is like a rutting elephant with tusks.”
The supreme elephant, Opavayha.
Descending from the back of the elephant,
the king, his mind intent on generosity, [proceeded].
The increaser of the Sivī kingdom gave gifts to the brahmins;
at that time there was a terrifying [event].
At that time, when the elephant-king was gifted, there was a bristling of the hair [with joy],
and the earth trembled all over.
Then there was that which was terrifying,
then there was that which caused the hair to stand on end,
when the noble elephant was given away.
Then the city was shaken;
the town was thoroughly agitated,
and there was a vast and great clamor.
When the elephant Hatthināga was gifted away,
increasing the kingdom of the Sivi people,
the Uggas and the princes—
Vaisyas and brahmins;
elephant-riders, cavalrymen,
charioteers, and infantrymen.
The entire town and the Śivis gathered together;
having seen the elephant being led away, they cried out.
They reported this to the king:
"O King, your son Vessantara is destroying your kingdom."
How could one give us the elephant,
the Naga honored by the kingdom?
How could one give us the tusker?
With tusks like elephant-goads,
broad-backed, knowing the field of battle,
all-white, the best of elephants.
Covered with a pale-white blanket,
its temples streaming, the crusher of enemies,
the elephant with its fly-whisk of a tusk.
White, resembling Mount Kelāsa, with its white parasol, its attendants,
its staff, and its elephant.
He gave to the brahmins an elephant that was a supreme vehicle for kings;
whoever should give food and drink, [that merit is great].
as well as robes and lodgings—
this indeed is the appropriate gift;
this indeed is worthy of the brahmins.
This is your royal lineage,
the increaser of the kingdom of the Sivi people;
how was Vessantara your son?
"O Sañjaya, he urges Gaja:
'If you do not carry out this word of the Śivis...'"
"I think the Sivi people will seize you along with your son.
"Let the kingdom perish;
I would rather go to hell."
Let even the kingdom perish; yet I will not,
at the word of the Sivi people,
[hand over] the prince who is innocent.
I would have him ordained from my own kingdom,
for he is my own biological son.
Let the country, if you wish, be without me.
Let even the kingdom perish; yet I will not,
at the word of the Sivi people,
[hand over] the prince who is innocent.
I would banish my own son from my kingdom, for he is my own biological offspring;
yet I would not betray him.
For he would bring ill repute upon me,
who am of noble virtue,
and he would produce much evil karma.
"How can we have our son Vessantara executed by the sword?
"Do not [strike] him with a staff or a sword."
For he is not worthy of imprisonment;
rather, banish him from the kingdom and let him dwell on the crooked mountain.
“If this is the desire of the Śivis,
we shall not reject that desire;
let him dwell here for this night.”
And let him enjoy sensual pleasures.
Then, at the end of that night,
toward the rising of the sun;
"Let the Śivis, becoming united,
banish him from the kingdom.
Arise, Kātyāyana, and depart with haste!"
"Go and say to Vessantara:
'O King, the Sivis are angry with you,
and the townspeople have assembled.'"
The Uggas and the princes,
the Vessikas and the Brahmins;
the elephant-riders and the charioteers—
Charioteers and infantrymen;
and even the entire town,
along with the Śivis, assembled together.
As the night fades away toward the rising of the sun,
let us be united and auspicious.
“They are banishing him from the kingdom.
Thus urged by King Śibi, he set out in haste as a messenger.
With hand-ornaments worn, well-clad,
and adorned with sandalwood paste,
he bathed his head in the water.
Wearing earrings of supreme jewels,
he approached the delightful city,
the residence of Vessantara.
There he saw the prince enjoying himself in his own city,
surrounded by his ministers.
Like Vāsava among the Thirty-three gods,
he went there in haste and spoke to Vessantara, saying: "Do it!"
“I shall experience suffering for you;
do not be angry with me, O bull among charioteers.
Having spoken thus, weeping, he prostrated himself.
The maker spoke to the king:
"You are my master, O Great King,
the provider of all desirable tastes."
"I shall experience suffering;
let the gods there comfort me, for those Śivis are angry with you."
And the guilds have assembled:
the Uggas, the princes,
the Vessikas, and the Brahmins.
Elephant-riders and those who serve in the ranks,
chariot-warriors and infantrymen,
as well as the entire town.
And the Śivayas gathered together from us at the end of night,
toward the rising of the sun.
“Having become united,
the Sivis banish him from the kingdom.
“In what am I angry with the Sivis?”
"I see no wrong-doing;
explain that to me, Katta:
why are they banishing me?"
The Uggas and the princes,
the Vessikas and the Brahmins,
the elephant-riders and the cavalrymen—
Charioteers and infantrymen;
they are censured for the gift of elephants,
and therefore they cause him to be expelled.
“I would give my heart and my eyes;
what use have I for external wealth?
Whether it be silver or gold,”
Pearls, beryl, and gems—
seeing my right arm extended when a supplicant had arrived—
I would give and not waver;
my mind delights in giving.
Even if all the Śivis [should seize] me, [I would still give].
Let them banish me or kill me;
I shall not desist from giving.
Let them cut me into seven pieces at their will.
Thus did the Sivis and the assembled townspeople say:
"On the bank of the Kontimārā river..."
Toward Mount Arañjara;
let him of good vows go by that same path by which those who have gone forth travel.”
“I shall go by that same path where the violators go;
forgive me for the night and day.”
“While I am giving this gift,” the king addressed Maddī,
who was beautiful in every limb.
“Whatever wealth or grain you possess that has been given by me—
whether it be silver or gold— ”
"Many pearls and beryl stones—
all that you should deposit,
as well as whatever paternal wealth you possess."
To him spoke the princess Maddī,
beautiful in all her limbs: "Where,
O Lord, shall I deposit it?"
"Being asked, tell me that.
"O Maddī, you should give gifts to those who possess virtue, according to their worth."
Indeed, there is no purpose higher than giving;
it is the foundation for all living beings.
O Maddī, you were compassionate toward your children.
Toward one's mother-in-law and father-in-law,
and toward him whom one considers a husband,
one should serve them with due respect.
If your husband should not think thus of you because of our separation,
seek another husband.
Do not grieve without me;
for I am going to the forest,
which is filled with terrible wild beasts.
"My life is in doubt,
being all alone in the great forest.
To her, the princess said:
Maddī, beautiful in every limb, said: "What are you saying to me?
You speak indeed an evil word."
It is not right, O Great King,
that you should go alone;
I too shall go with you.
Whither you go, O Kṣatriya—
whether it be death with you,
or life without you.
Death itself would be better for me than to live without you.
Having kindled a fire—
United by a single bond;
therein death would be better for me than life without you.
Just as a female elephant follows the forest-dwelling tusker as he roams through the mountain fastnesses, so does she follow him.
On even ground and on uneven;
thus I follow after you,
taking my children with me.
I shall be easy for you to maintain; I will not be difficult for you to maintain.
Beholding these princes...
To Mañjuke, who speaks so pleasantly,
as he sits within the forest thicket,
you will not remember the kingdom.
Beholding these youths,
gentle and sweet-spoken,
playing in the forest thicket—
You will not remember Rajja while seeing these princes,
so charming and sweet-spoken.
In this delightful forest,
you will not remember the kingdom;
for you shall see these princes.
O sweet-spoken one who speaks kindly!
While sporting in this delightful hermitage,
you will not remember the kingdom.
Seeing these two youths,
wearing garlands and adorned with ornaments,
in that delightful hermitage,
You will not remember the rope while beholding these princes,
adorned and wearing garlands.
Playing in delightful hermitages,
you will not remember kingship when you see them dancing.
While you are a prince wearing a garland,
in a delightful hermitage,
you will not remember the kingdom.
When you see the young princes, wearing garlands,
dancing and sporting in the delightful hermitage,
You will not remember the rope when you see Mātanga,
the sixty-year-old elephant.
When you see Mātaṅga wandering alone in the forest, you will not remember the kingdom.
An elephant sixty years of age,
roaming about evening and morning—
you will not remember him as being bound by a rope.
When the elephant, the lord of the herd,
trumpets loudly in front of the troop of female elephants, he leads the way.
An elephant sixty years of age—
having heard him trumpeting,
you will no longer remember the kingdom.
When you see the grove of desire expanding on both sides,
in that forest teeming with predatory beasts,
You will not remember the rope.
Having seen the deer in the evening,
Pañcamāliṇa has arrived.
While the kimpurisas dance,
you will not remember the kingdom;
when you hear their clamor, [you will remember it].
Flowing along with the river,
you will remember the song of the *kimpurisas*,
not that of the king.
When you hear the cry of the owl dwelling within the mountain caves as it hoots,
You will not remember the cord.
When [you see] the lion, the tiger,
the rhinoceros, and the gayal;
In the forest you will hear the cries of wild beasts,
and you will not remember the kingdom;
when you are surrounded by peahens—
You will see a peacock with its tail-feathers lost, standing on its head and dancing;
you will not remember the king's rule.
When you see the egg-born peacock dancing, surrounded by its peahens, its wings variegated—
You will not remember the rope when you see the crested peacock with its blue neck,
surrounded by peahens.
You will see a peacock dancing,
and you will not remember the king. When you see it in winter, [you will forget].
When the trees are in bloom and wafting forth fragrant scents,
you will not remember kingship.
When, in the month of winter,
you see the Medani forest green and covered with *indagopaka* insects,
you will know that the rains have come.
You will not remember the rope when you see the trees in bloom during the winter.
The *kuṭaja*, the cluster of *bimba* flowers,
the blooming *loddha* and *padmaka*,
and the fragrant [trees] waft their scent abroad.
You will not remember the cord when you see the forest in bloom during the winter months.
And the lotus flowers—
you will not remember them for the sake of wealth.
This is called "The Snowy Mountains."
3. The Chapter on Giving (Dānakaṇḍa) Having heard the lamentation of those two,
the son and the daughter-in-law;
The illustrious princess lamented piteously:
“Better for me would it have been to swallow poison, than to live without my husband.”
I have fallen, I might fall;
bound by a rope, I shall die—
why [should I not give up] my son Vessantara?
They cause one who is innocent to go forth—
one who is a reciter of the scriptures, a master of giving,
devoted to making requests, and free from stinginess.
Why did you abandon your son Vessantara, who was honored by rival kings and possessed of great renown and fame?
They cause one who is innocent to go forth—
one who supports his mother and father,
and who honors those who are senior in the family.
Why do they exile the blameless son Vessantara,
who is beneficial to the king and beneficial to the queen?
He is beneficial to his kinsmen and friends;
he is beneficial to the entire kingdom—
why then [banish] Vessantara, your son?
They cause one who is innocent to go forth,
like honeycombs that have been plundered,
or like mangoes fallen to the ground.
In this way your kingdom will become such that they banish even the innocent,
like a swan whose feathers have been plucked out.
In a waterless marsh,
abandoned by your ministers,
you stand alone, O King, deprived of all.
I say this to you, O Great King:
let not your welfare pass you by;
do not, because of the words of the Sivis, neglect it.
He ordained one who was innocent.
"I honor the Dhamma,
the banner of the discipline of the Sivis."
“I am ordaining my own son,
for he is dearer to me than life itself.
“For whom, in former times, the tips of banners...”
The Kaṇikāra trees are in full bloom;
they follow him as he goes, thinking,
"He will depart this very day."
For whomsoever, as they go along,
the banners follow like groves of *kaṇikāra* trees.
He will go to Svajjekova.
He for whom the armies were formerly like blossoming *kaṇikāra* trees.
Though they follow him as he goes,
he will depart alone this very day;
for him whose armies were formerly [many], [now there is none].
Like bees following a *kaṇikāra* grove,
they follow him as he departs;
tomorrow alone he will go.
With the luster of the indagopaka insect,
like Gandhāra rugs or pale blankets,
they follow him as he goes.
He will go by means of a palanquin.
He who formerly traveled by elephant,
by palanquin, and by chariot;
How is it that today King Vessantara goes on foot?
How is it that his body is smeared with sandalwood paste?
Awakened by dancing and singing,
he will carry a razor, a hide,
an axe, and a carrying-pole.
Why would they not offer him saffron robes and antelope skins as he enters the great forest?
Why are their robes not fastened?
How indeed do these people who have gone forth from royal families wear their robes?
How will Maddī wear coarse garments made of grass,
after having worn those from Kāsī?
Wearing hempen garments and rags from dust heaps,
how will Maddī fare?
Having been carried about on litters,
in palanquins, and in chariots—
how is it that today she is being carried away?
She goes along the path on foot—
she whose hands have soft palms and whose feet are well-nourished.
Today she goes on foot along the road,
her feet so tender and soft.
Her feet were raised in comfort,
yet she walked as if her feet were being crushed by golden sandals.
Today she goes on foot along the road,
having lost her status as one of those thousands of women.
Mālinī was walking ahead;
she went alone today to the forest, heedless and without a companion.
That speech which, having heard for the sake of welfare,
one used to tremble at even momentarily—
how could that speech today not be abandoned?
The timid ones go to the forest—
those who belong to the clan of Indra,
while the owl is crying out.
Having heard them roaring,
she trembled in fear like a female crocodile;
how could she today remain unconcerned?
She goes to the forest like a timid bird that,
seeing its nest empty, has had her young killed.
I shall meditate on suffering for a long time,
having come to this empty city,
like a bird whose young have been killed.
Seeing the bird's nest empty,
I shall become thin and pale,
not seeing my dear children.
Like a bird whose chicks have been killed,
seeing her nest empty,
I shall run hither and thither.
He will not see his beloved children,
like a kurarī bird whose chicks have been killed,
seeing her nest empty.
I shall meditate on suffering for a long time,
having come to this empty city,
like a female osprey whose chicks have been slain.
Seeing the bird's nest empty,
I shall become thin and pale,
not seeing my dear children.
The female osprey, her bow broken,
seeing her nest empty,
will run here and there.
She will not see her beloved sons;
she is surely like a female ruddy goose in a pond that has run dry.
I shall meditate on suffering for a long time,
having come to this empty city.
Surely she is like a female ruddy goose...
In a waterless marsh,
I shall become emaciated and pale,
not seeing my beloved children.
Surely like a female ruddy goose in a pond that has run dry,
I shall run hither and thither.
She will not see her beloved sons.
Thus, as I lament,
the king [will take] his innocent son.
"She has been banished from the kingdom to the forest;
I fear she will lose her life.
Having heard her lamentation, [he said:]
Many women within the inner apartments,
having raised their arms, cried out together as the daughter of Sivi arrived.
Shaken like a sal tree and crushed by a tempestuous wind,
sons and wives lie prostrate.
In the residence of Vessantara,
there were male servants and princes,
courtesans and brahmins.
Raising their arms and crying out in the residence of Vessantara,
the elephant-riders and those stationed in the army—
Charioteers and infantrymen raised their arms and cried out at the residence of Vessantara.
Then, at the end of the night,
as the sun was rising,
King Vessantara—
He approached to give a gift:
"Give garments to those who desire garments;
give liquor to the drunkards."
Give food properly to those who seek food; do not [neglect] any mendicant.
They have been tormented upon arriving here;
satisfy them with food and drink,
and let them depart duly honored.
Then a loud, terrifying, and great noise arose there:
"They are carrying him out by means of a gift!"
Once again you gave alms.
Those beggars, intoxicated as it were and exhausted, fell down.
As the great king, the prosperer of the Sivi realm, was departing, [they cried]:
"Alas, they have cut down the tree!"
Just as they banish from the kingdom Vessantara, though he is innocent, like a tree bearing various fruits.
Alas, they have indeed cut down the tree,
that wish-fulfilling tree,
just as they have banished Vessantara from the kingdom!
They cause one who is innocent to go forth.
Alas, they have cut down the tree that brings the essence of all desires!
Just as they banish Vessantara from the kingdom,
though he is innocent—
both those who are old and those who are young.
And those of middle stature,
stretching out their arms,
cried out as the Great King was departing.
In the kingdom of the Sivis,
the rain-giving clouds poured down excessively,
as did the king’s women of the harem.
Raising their arms and crying out as the Great Kings were departing,
they lamented for the one who increases the realm of the Śivis.
Even the women who were there in that city cried out as the great king was departing.
In the kingdom of the Sivi people,
whatever brahmins, ascetics,
or other mendicants there may be—
Raising his arms and crying out,
"Indeed, this is unrighteousness!
Just as King Vessantara..."
The sacrificer, in his own city,
is driven out from the kingdom by the word of the Śivīs.
Having given seven hundred elephants adorned with every ornament,
those tuskers with golden girths.
When he had mounted his golden-hued elephant, which was led by village chiefs holding spears and goads in their hands;
This King Vessantara is being banished from the kingdom after giving away seven hundred horses.
Adorned with every ornament,
like noble Sindhu horses of pure breed, swift in their course.
When Vessantara the king had mounted, together with the village headmen who were carrying their quivers and bows—
He was expelled from his kingdom.
Having given away seven hundred chariots,
he departed clad in armor with banners raised high.
And also on the island of Veyaggha,
mounted upon elephants adorned with every ornament by the village chiefs.
By armored men with bows in their hands—
this King Vessantara is being banished from the kingdom.
Having given seven hundred women,
each standing upon a chariot,
equipped with armor and golden girths.
Adorned with gold,
wearing yellow ornaments and yellow garments,
they were embellished with yellow jewelry.
With long, reddish-brown hair, beautiful eyes,
a clear consciousness, and a slender waist—
this is King Vessantara.
He was banished from the kingdom of Saṃhāra.
Having given seven hundred cows,
all of which had brass milking vessels, he departed.
This King Vessantara is being banished from the kingdom,
having given away seven hundred female slaves.
And seven hundred slaves—
this King Vessantara is being banished from the kingdom.
Having given elephants, horse-chariots,
and adorned women—
this is King Vessantara.
He was banished from his own country.
That was a terrifying thing;
that was hair-raising.
When the great gift was bestowed,
the earth trembled all over;
at that time there was a terrifying occurrence.
Then there was a hair-raising terror,
as the king, with palms joined in reverence,
was driven out from the kingdom.
Then a sound arose there, tumultuous,
terrifying, and great;
they carry him out by means of a gift.
Again you gave alms.
Those beggars, intoxicated as it were and exhausted, fell down.
As the Great King,
the increaser of the Sivi realm,
was departing, he addressed the monarch:
To Sañjaya, the best of the righteous:
“O King, you have imprisoned me;
I am going to Mount Vaṅka.”
For whoever, O Great King,
have been beings or will be, they remain indeed unsatisfied with sensual pleasures.
They go to the realm of Yama.
May I, performing sacrifice in my own city, attain my own reward.
Because of the words of the Śivis,
I was expelled from the kingdom;
I shall experience that misfortune.
In the forest, thick with wild beasts and frequented by rhinoceroses and leopards,
I perform meritorious deeds.
"You are sinking in the mire.
Grant me permission, mother;
renunciation is what I desire."
I shall sacrifice for myself in my own city,
performing the sacrifice for myself,
in accordance with the words of the Śivis.
I have been driven out from my kingdom.
I shall endure that calamity in the forest, which is teeming with wild beasts.
While I perform meritorious deeds, served by those who possess the wisdom of the rhinoceros,
you sink into the mire.
“I grant you permission, my son;
may your going forth be successful;
and this Maddī, the virtuous one—”
She has beautiful consciousness and a slender waist;
she will live happily with her sons—
what will she do in the forest?
“I cannot bear to lead even a slave girl to the forest against her will;
if she so desires, let her follow.”
"If she desires it, let her have it.
Then the Great King proceeded to ask his daughter-in-law.
“O you whose conduct is like sandalwood,
do not wear dust and dirt.
Do not wear garments of kasiya cloth;”
He wore a garment of kusa grass;
dwelling in the forest is painful,
so do not go to Lakkhaṇa.
To him spoke the princess Maddī,
beautiful in every limb:
"I would not desire that happiness for myself."
"Without my Vessantara," [he said].
To him, the Great King,
the increaser of the Sivi realm, replied:
"Come now, Madri, listen to those things that are difficult to endure in the forest:
there are many insects and moths."
There are honey-bees that sting;
they too would harm one there,
and that would be even more painful for you.
Look at another place,
a scorched land frequented by rivers,
where snakes called ajagaras dwell.
Those mighty ones are not careless;
whether it be a human or even a deer,
they do not overlook one who has come near.
Having surrounded them with their possessions,
they bring others under their own control—
others who likewise wear matted hair, black in hue.
The so-called "smooth" are indeed the snares of evil;
a man is not released from them merely by climbing a tree.
Butting their horns together,
striking with sharp-pointed tips,
the buffaloes roam about here.
Toward the Sotumbara River.
Having seen herds of deer and cattle roaming in the forest, [he approached].
Like a cow greedy for her calf,
Maddī, how will you fare when you see those two terrible ones fallen?
O Maddī, when you encounter monkeys on difficult paths,
great danger will befall you,
for they do not know the proper way to treat guests.
You who formerly trembled repeatedly upon hearing the word "snake," you have now reached a crooked fate.
How will you manage it, Maddī,
when the time of midday has arrived and the birds have settled down?
“The vast forest rustles;
why do you wish to go there?
To her, the princess replied:
Maddī, beautiful in every limb,
said: “Those things which you have described to me as fearsome in the forest;”
I overcame them all as I went along,
O bull among charioteers:
kāsa, kusa, and poṭakila.
Like usīra grass, muñja grass, or pabbaja grass,
I shall push you away with my chest;
perish, for I shall be free from bad conduct!
Indeed, through many kinds of conduct,
a maiden finds a husband;
even by the restraint of her belly [she may do so].
And by wrapping the calves with a cloth;
by attending upon the fire,
and by swimming in water;
O Bull among Charioteers, as you go forth, even that which is to be pierced and is pungent in this world remains unattained by you.
Even when one has finished eating,
he who seizes him by the hand and drags him away against his will;
O Bull among Charioteers, as you depart, you will experience in this world the piercing pain of having your hair seized and pulled.
And trampling upon the ground; having given [a gift], one does not exert oneself [to maintain it];
this brings much suffering that is not small.
